title: 48 hours of one machine breakdown, from first alarm to root cause
summary: A fictional two-day failure on a fictional line: the clock and the cause both matter, and the first suspect is wrong.

blocks.title: Two days, one overload alarm, three wrong suspects
blocks.body: The filler on Line 3 tripped its overload at 06:12 on a Monday. It was running again by Wednesday breakfast, but the part that matters is what happened between: when the clock was spent on suspects and when it was spent on evidence.

blocks.title: This incident is invented
blocks.body: The line, the machine, the people, and the times are fictional, built to show a real pattern: breakdowns have a timeline and a causal chain, and confusing the two is how hours get lost.

items.title: Overload trip
items.detail: Filler drive faults out mid-cycle. Operator resets; it trips again in four minutes. Line down.

items.title: Suspect one: the motor
items.detail: It is warm and it is the thing the alarm named. Megger test says the windings are fine. Two hours spent.

items.title: Suspect two: the drive
items.detail: Swapped with the spare from the crib. Same trip, same four minutes. The drive was telling the truth both times.

items.title: The question changes
items.detail: From what failed to what is it protecting against. Current trace shows the draw climbing over ninety seconds before every trip.

items.title: Suspect three: the product
items.detail: A thicker syrup ran all weekend. Flushed and ran water - still trips. Not the product. Shift ends; the night crew babysits.

items.title: Hands on the machine
items.detail: Guards off, turned by hand. A tight spot once per revolution of the main cam.

items.title: Found it
items.detail: A bearing on the cam shaft has brinelled - dented races from months of hammering during a misaligned changeover. The tight spot loads the drive until the overload saves the motor.

items.title: Repair
items.detail: Bearing pressed off and replaced, shaft checked, alignment shimmed to the print.

items.title: Proof
items.detail: Two hours at rate, current trace flat. The trace, not the silence, is the evidence.

items.title: Back in the schedule
items.detail: 48 hours after the first alarm. The line runs; the write-up begins.

blocks.heading: The causal chain, minus the clock

nodes.title: Root cause
nodes.detail: Brinelled cam-shaft bearing, from months of misalignment shock loads.

nodes.title: Mechanism
nodes.detail: A tight spot once per revolution raises mechanical load.

nodes.title: Signal
nodes.detail: Drive current climbs over ninety seconds until the overload trips.

nodes.title: Symptom
nodes.detail: The alarm names the motor - the victim, not the cause.

blocks.heading: Two clocks were running
blocks.body: The wall clock says 48 hours. The diagnostic clock says about five: the megger test, the drive swap, the current trace, the hand-turn, the bearing press. The other forty-three were queue time, shift changes, and waiting on the crib. When the post-mortem asks why it took two days, the answer is mostly not troubleshooting - and that answer is what makes the next one faster.

blocks.heading: What each suspect cost and taught
rows: Rule out what the alarm names first - quickly, on purpose
A spare swap is expensive proof; the identical failure was the clue
Coincidence is not causation, but it had to be tested, not argued
Found by hand, not by instrument - the tight spot was physical

blocks.heading: What the write-up changed
items: Current traces get pulled in the first hour now, not the second day - the ninety-second climb was visible from the start.
Changeover alignment gets a torque-and-shim check on the PM sheet, because the brinelling had an author.
The crib's spare drive gets a tag: last known good, date - so a swap is evidence, not a gamble.
Hand-turning the machine moved up the checklist, above parts-swapping.

blocks.heading: Check the lesson
blocks.prompt: The overload named the motor, and the motor tested fine. What is the correct next frame?
options: Ask what the protection is protecting against - the trip is data
Replace the motor anyway, since the alarm named it
Reset and run until it trips again to see if it is consistent
blocks.explanation: A protective trip is a measurement: something downstream asked for more than the limit. When the named component is innocent, the alarm was still telling the truth about the load.
